newsitem.title: USA: NYS senate says casino bill won't be reconsidered.
newsitem.headline: NYS senate says casino bill won't be reconsidered.

text.p: The New York State Senate, which on Tuesday defeated a bill to allow casino gambling by a margin of 41 to 19, said that the measure would not be considered again in 1997 or 1998.

"The vote on casino gambling will be the last vote taken on this particular resolution during the 1997 legislative session. This constitutional amendment is dead and will not be considered again either this year or next year," said Senate Majority Leader Joseph Bruno (R-Troy), in prepared remarks.
Bruno told reporters in Albany that while a new proposal could be voted on next year, it was unlikely such a vote would be held, saying, "Yes, we could, but the anticipation is that we won't."

He explained that when it became apparent that the Democrats, whose support was needed to secure the bill's approval, were not coming out in force to support it, he opted to leave his members free to vote as they believed best.

The Senate Majority Leader is not a supporter of gambling though he had urged lawmakers to send the proposal to the voters in a referendum, as would have been required had it for a second time won approval from the Senate and the House.
He suggested contributions from lobbyists had influenced votes but defended the practice.

"Well, the apparent result would indicate that somebody had some success, because I thought that there would be more support in the senate for taking this to a referendum to the people," he said, when asked if real estate tycoon Donald Trump's contributions had had an impact.

Trump, who owns the Taj Mahal casino resort in Atlantic City, New Jersey, in 1996 spent $855,750 to fight the measure and had signed contracts to spend at least that sum in 1997, the New York Times said on Monday.

A supporter of the bill, Nicholas Spano (R-Westchester), told reporters in Albany that it was flawed as it did not include New York City or riverboats. Other lawmakers said they objected because they do not approve of gambling.

The bill would have allowed one casino to be built in Niagara Falls, Buffalo and either Warren or Saratoga Counties, plus an unlimited number in the Catskills, whose resorts are losing ground to casinos in Atlantic City and Connecticut. Gov George Pataki, who supported the bill, has said the state was losing billions of dollars to out-of-state casinos and ones run by Native Americans in the state.
